excerpt: What limits apply to a South Carolina medical malpractice claim, how damages are treated, and the deadlines that govern filing.
keyTakeaways: South Carolina caps non-economic damages in medical malpractice cases at $596,001 per provider or institution and $1,788,002 in total for 2026, figures adjusted each year for inflation (S.C. Code § 15-32-220). The statute of limitations is three years (S.C. Code § 15-3-545) with a six-year statute of repose. Before filing suit, plaintiffs must file a Notice of Intent together with an expert affidavit, serve it on each defendant, and mediate; only if mediation fails can the lawsuit be filed (S.C. Code § 15-79-125). Economic damages (medical bills, lost wages) are uncapped. These procedural requirements make early legal involvement essential.

faqs.question: Does South Carolina cap damages in medical malpractice cases?
faqs.answer: Yes. South Carolina caps non-economic damages at a base of $350,000 per provider or institution and $1,050,000 in total per claimant, adjusted each year for inflation: for 2026, $596,001 and $1,788,002 (S.C. Code § 15-32-220). There is no cap on economic damages like medical bills and lost wages. Punitive damages are capped at three times compensatory damages or $739,245, the 2026 inflation-indexed figure, whichever is greater (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a medical malpractice lawsuit in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: South Carolina imposes a three-year statute of limitations (S.C. Code § 15-3-545) from the date of the negligent act or from when the injury was or should have been discovered. A six-year statute of repose generally applies — in most cases no claim can be filed more than six years after the negligence occurred.

faqs.question: What is the Notice of Intent to File Suit requirement in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: Under S.C. Code § 15-79-125, before filing a malpractice lawsuit you must file a Notice of Intent to File Suit together with a qualified expert's affidavit (S.C. Code § 15-36-100), and serve it on each defendant. Filing the notice tolls the statute of limitations. The parties must then mediate, generally within 90 to 120 days of service, before the lawsuit can be filed.

faqs.question: Is mediation required in South Carolina medical malpractice cases?
faqs.answer: Yes. South Carolina requires mandatory mediation in medical malpractice cases before the lawsuit is filed (S.C. Code § 15-79-125). A neutral mediator attempts to facilitate a settlement. If mediation is unsuccessful, the lawsuit can then be filed.

faqs.question: What is the statute of repose for medical malpractice in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: South Carolina's six-year statute of repose (S.C. Code § 15-3-545) generally bars a medical malpractice lawsuit filed more than six years after the negligent act, even if the injury was not discovered until later. This is more generous than Georgia's five-year repose period but still bars some legitimate claims.

faqs.question: Can I sue a hospital for medical malpractice in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: Yes. Hospitals, medical centers, individual physicians, nurses, specialists, pharmacies, and nursing homes can all be sued for medical malpractice in South Carolina. Each provider or institution is subject to its own non-economic damage cap ($596,001 for 2026), up to $1,788,002 in total for all defendants combined (S.C. Code § 15-32-220), which is why identifying all liable parties is critical to maximizing your total recovery.
